question: How do the portfolio's valuations compare with public peers?
html:
Portfolio Valuations vs. Public Peers

The context cannot give a direct valuation comparison. The public peer set reports growth, margins and revenue per employee, not trading multiples. BSP's current marks are also not in the context. What it does show is how the portfolio's operating profiles line up with peers, and which private-deal multiples buyers pay.

What the data covers

  • Public peers: 31 companies, with GAAP operating metrics only. EBITDA is operating income plus D&A, not adjusted EBITDA (Public comparables).
  • Private deal evidence: banker grids and press-reported deals. Capstone/IMAP put typical middle-market deals at 6.8x and premium deals at 9.8x (ServiceOS evidence).
  • Portfolio marks: none, apart from an estimated ~12-15x entry for Frontline (est.) (ServiceOS evidence).

Benchmarks by portfolio company

Portfolio companyPublic peer profilePrivate multiple evidenceQuality premium (est.)
Punctual ProsResidential peers: 13.6% median growth, 15.1% EBITDA margin; installers flat at +1.0-1.5%PKF 5-6x project-heavy vs 10x+ repeatable; Champions ~18.5x, Sila ~17x at scale1.0-2.5 turns
CETCommercial electrical: 6.4% median operating margin, ~11.2% EBITDA; 16.8% revenue CAGRPKF grid; 99 electrical deals in 20250.5-1.5 turns
FrontlineOnshore services earn 3-9% margins (CBIZ $290k revenue per employee)Aventis MSP curve 5.2x-11.2x0.5-1.5 turns
Thomas ScientificDistribution peers (Avantor)No disclosed multiple premium; capital structure dominates0.5-1.0 turns
BPIAgencies ex-growth: median +0.3%, WPP -8.1%PPHC ~8.4x floor vs 10-13x est. sponsor exit0.5-2.0 turns
Fair HarborNot shown in contextNot shown in contextRange truncated in source

How to read this

  • Trades have thin public margins. Value creation comes from mix, such as service and mission-critical work, more than price (Public comparables).
  • Up to ~3 turns of quality premium are supported. Tech enablement can claim about 0.5-2.5 turns of that (ServiceOS evidence).
  • The 17-20x roll-up prints reflect scale. They come from scale, density and M&A runway, not technology alone. They are also unconfirmed press estimates (ServiceOS evidence).
  • Frontline's peers point to modest economics. A US-heavy services company should expect CBIZ-like margins unless it adds offshore leverage (Public comparables).

Data needed to answer directly

  • EV/EBITDA and EV/revenue for all 31 peers, at a stated date.
  • Each portfolio company's latest mark, LTM adjusted EBITDA and net debt.
  • A bridge from GAAP peer EBITDA to company-defined adjusted EBITDA.

Next actions

  1. Add trading multiples to the public comparables set, dated to a single close (e.g., Oct 16, 2026).
  2. Pull current marks and LTM adjusted EBITDA for the six portfolio companies from the latest valuation pack.
  3. Build a multiple bridge for each portfolio company: peer trading multiple, then private-deal discount or premium, then the estimated quality premium.
  4. Fill the Fair Harbor gap with consumer apparel peers and the full HarborOS premium range.

# Portfolio Valuations vs. Public Peers

**The context cannot give a direct valuation comparison.** The public peer set reports growth, margins and revenue per employee, not trading multiples. BSP's current marks are also not in the context. What it does show is how the portfolio's operating profiles line up with peers, and which private-deal multiples buyers pay.

## What the data covers

- **Public peers:** 31 companies, with GAAP operating metrics only. EBITDA is operating income plus D&A, not adjusted EBITDA (Public comparables).
- **Private deal evidence:** banker grids and press-reported deals. Capstone/IMAP put typical middle-market deals at 6.8x and premium deals at 9.8x (ServiceOS evidence).
- **Portfolio marks:** none, apart from an estimated ~12-15x entry for Frontline (est.) (ServiceOS evidence).

## Benchmarks by portfolio company

| Portfolio company | Public peer profile | Private multiple evidence | Quality premium (est.) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Punctual Pros | Residential peers: 13.6% median growth, 15.1% EBITDA margin; installers flat at +1.0-1.5% | PKF 5-6x project-heavy vs 10x+ repeatable; Champions ~18.5x, Sila ~17x at scale | 1.0-2.5 turns |
| CET | Commercial electrical: 6.4% median operating margin, ~11.2% EBITDA; 16.8% revenue CAGR | PKF grid; 99 electrical deals in 2025 | 0.5-1.5 turns |
| Frontline | Onshore services earn 3-9% margins (CBIZ $290k revenue per employee) | Aventis MSP curve 5.2x-11.2x | 0.5-1.5 turns |
| Thomas Scientific | Distribution peers (Avantor) | No disclosed multiple premium; capital structure dominates | 0.5-1.0 turns |
| BPI | Agencies ex-growth: median +0.3%, WPP -8.1% | PPHC ~8.4x floor vs 10-13x est. sponsor exit | 0.5-2.0 turns |
| Fair Harbor | Not shown in context | Not shown in context | Range truncated in source |

## How to read this

- **Trades have thin public margins.** Value creation comes from mix, such as service and mission-critical work, more than price (Public comparables).
- **Up to ~3 turns of quality premium are supported.** Tech enablement can claim about 0.5-2.5 turns of that (ServiceOS evidence).
- **The 17-20x roll-up prints reflect scale.** They come from scale, density and M&A runway, not technology alone. They are also unconfirmed press estimates (ServiceOS evidence).
- **Frontline's peers point to modest economics.** A US-heavy services company should expect CBIZ-like margins unless it adds offshore leverage (Public comparables).

## Data needed to answer directly

- EV/EBITDA and EV/revenue for all 31 peers, at a stated date.
- Each portfolio company's latest mark, LTM adjusted EBITDA and net debt.
- A bridge from GAAP peer EBITDA to company-defined adjusted EBITDA.

## Next actions

1. Add trading multiples to the public comparables set, dated to a single close (e.g., Oct 16, 2026).
2. Pull current marks and LTM adjusted EBITDA for the six portfolio companies from the latest valuation pack.
3. Build a multiple bridge for each portfolio company: peer trading multiple, then private-deal discount or premium, then the estimated quality premium.
4. Fill the Fair Harbor gap with consumer apparel peers and the full HarborOS premium range.
